intro: Read the deck for the law and these notes for the thinking. Each note says what a slide is for, how to hold it in memory and where practitioners slip. Work the calculations in pencil, test yourself with the recall questions, and check every threshold against the primary source before you advise anyone.

sections.title: The Mandate: why corporate giving here is a legal duty
sections.big_idea: In India a company in scope **must spend**, and must document it. CSR, ESG and sustainability are three different things.
in_plain_words: Voluntary guidelines in 2009 and 2011 drew thin take-up, so the Companies Act 2013 made a minimum spend a statutory duty, in force from 1 April 2014. For a company in scope, CSR is compliance. That changes who is accountable, what must be documented, which deadlines apply and what happens to unspent money, and it is why most international CSR writing does not transfer.

The minimum is 2% of average net profit over three years, and the national total was ₹34,909 crore in FY2023-24. CSR is a statutory spending duty, ESG is a disclosure frame for investors, and sustainability is a description. The law is praised for predictable money and criticised as a tax without democratic allocation. **Both critiques are argued seriously**, and the course expects you to hold both.

events.what: Section 135 and CSR Rules in force

key_terms.meaning: In India, a statutory spending and reporting duty under Section 135.
Environmental, social and governance: a disclosure frame mostly for investors.
The broadest and least precise word; often a description or marketing.
The Companies Act 2013 provision creating the CSR obligation.
National Voluntary Guidelines of 2011, the step before the statute.

worked_example.title: Scale one firm against the national total
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's own example: a firm averaging ₹100 crore of net profit. The national total is ₹34,909 crore (FY2023-24) and the rural employment guarantee gets ₹95,692 crore in Budget 2026-27.
steps: The firm's minimum spend: 100 × 0.02 = 2 crore.
National CSR as a share of the single scheme: 34,909 ÷ 95,692 = 36.5%.
Gap between the two: 95,692 − 34,909 = 60,783 crore.
Read it plainly: all corporate CSR is about a third of one public scheme.
worked_example.answer: ₹2 crore for the example firm, and national CSR equal to about 36.5% of the rural employment guarantee allocation.

mistakes: Using 'CSR', 'ESG' and 'sustainability' as synonyms when they carry three duties, audiences and legal statuses.
Reading international CSR writing as if Indian CSR were voluntary philanthropy.
Forgetting that this year's obligation was fixed by profits from the three years already reported.
Teaching only the mechanics and skipping the critique, which produces compliance officers instead of practitioners.

recall.q: Which Act made CSR a legal duty in India?
recall.a: The Companies Act 2013, Section 135.

recall.q: What is the minimum spend?
recall.a: 2% of average net profit over the three immediately preceding financial years.

recall.q: What was the national CSR total in FY2023-24?
Name one argument for and one against the mandate.
recall.a: For: predictable money at scale. Against: a tax without democratic allocation.

recall.q: Which country mandated corporate social spending before India?
recall.a: Mauritius, from 2009.

sections.title: Who Is Bound: Section 135, and the threshold that catches you
sections.big_idea: Any **one** of three thresholds binds, tested on the year just ended. Scope and the amount use different windows.
in_plain_words: Section 135(1) covers every company, including a foreign company's Indian branch or project office, that meets any one of three tests in the immediately preceding financial year: net worth of ₹500 crore or more, turnover of ₹1,000 crore or more, or net profit of ₹5 crore or more. Reading the tests as cumulative is the commonest error.

Scope reads one year. The amount reads the average of three preceding years. Since 20 September 2022 there is no three-year exit lag, so entry and exit are immediate. Net profit means the Section 198 figure, excluding overseas-branch profit and dividends from covered, complying Indian companies. **In scope and owing money are separate questions**: a loss-making company in scope still owes governance.

diagram.root: In scope if any one test is met
diagram.caption: tested on the immediately preceding financial year

key_terms.meaning: A balance-sheet threshold of ₹500 crore or more.
A revenue threshold of ₹1,000 crore or more.
Profit computed under Section 198, with CSR-specific exclusions.
The statements from which a foreign company's Indian figures are taken.
The single year just ended, used for the scope test.
Leaving scope when none of the three thresholds is met in the preceding year.

worked_example.title: How close is a company to the line?
worked_example.setup: Epsilon Ltd is an illustrative company with net worth ₹450 crore, turnover ₹980 crore and net profit ₹4 crore in the year just ended.
steps: Net worth shortfall: 500 − 450 = 50 crore.
Turnover shortfall: 1,000 − 980 = 20 crore.
Profit shortfall: 5 − 4 = 1 crore.
None of the three is met, so Epsilon is out of scope for the next year.
It must test itself afresh every year, because a rise in any one figure brings it back in.
worked_example.answer: Epsilon is out of scope this year, and a turnover rise of just over 20 crore would bring it in.

mistakes: Reading the three thresholds as cumulative and telling a company it is exempt.
Computing the amount owed on the scope year instead of the average of three preceding years.
Assuming a foreign multinational is exempt, when its Indian branch is tested on Indian figures.
Treating a loss-making company in scope as owing nothing at all, when committee, policy, plan and report remain.

recall.q: Which window decides scope?
recall.a: The immediately preceding financial year alone.

recall.q: Which window decides the amount?
recall.a: The average of the three immediately preceding financial years.

recall.q: What happened to Rule 3(2) on 20 September 2022?
recall.a: It was omitted, so a company meeting no threshold is out of scope for the next year.

recall.q: Which profits does the CSR net profit exclude?
recall.a: Overseas-branch profit, and dividends from covered Indian companies that comply with Section 135.

recall.q: Why can Beta Ltd in the deck owe nothing and still be in scope?
recall.a: It is in scope on turnover, but its average net profit is nil.

sections.title: The Boundary Question: Schedule VII, and what does not count
sections.big_idea: Schedule VII is the gate, read liberally. Most disputes ask **who benefits** and whether the company would have spent the money anyway.
in_plain_words: Schedule VII lists the activities a company may include in its CSR policy: hunger, health and sanitation; education and livelihoods; gender equality; environment; heritage; veterans; sport; government funds; incubators and R&D; rural development and disaster management. Spending outside it is not CSR expenditure, however worthy.

The MCA says to read the entries liberally for their essence, which is different from anything goes. The exclusions are activities outside India, staff-only benefits, political contributions, normal-course business, marketing sponsorship and other statutory obligations. The last two do the most work. **Argue boundary cases in writing**, naming the entry and its essence, because that is what an auditor looks for.

left.title: Generally accepted
items: Skilling open to the wider community
Rural drinking water near a plant
Restoring a water body the firm does not own

right.title: Generally rejected
items: Work done in the normal course of business
Effluent treatment already required by law

key_terms.meaning: The list of activities that count as CSR expenditure.
Interpreting an entry by its essence, as the MCA instructs.
Activity the company would do commercially; excluded.
Spending already legally required; cannot be counted twice.
Asking who benefits and whether the company would have spent anyway.

worked_example.title: Argue four boundary cases
worked_example.setup: Apply the deck's two questions (who is the beneficiary, would this be spent regardless) to four illustrative projects.
steps: A skilling course open to the wider community near a plant: beneficiaries are wide, so probably CSR.
A course that only feeds the company's hiring pipeline: the company benefits, so probably not CSR.
Effluent treatment the company must do anyway: another statutory obligation, so excluded.
A crèche for employees only: staff welfare, so excluded.
worked_example.answer: The first is probably CSR and the other three are excluded, each for a named reason.

mistakes: Treating Schedule VII as twelve rigid boxes, which rejects sound projects.
Treating it as infinitely elastic, which approves anything.
Counting spending a company was already required to make as CSR.
Asking whether a project is good, when almost everything on both lists is good.

recall.q: What does the MCA say about reading Schedule VII?
recall.a: Interpret it liberally, to capture the essence of the subjects listed.

recall.q: Name three exclusions from CSR.
recall.a: Any three of: outside India, employee-only benefit, political contributions, normal-course business, marketing sponsorship, other statutory obligation.

recall.q: Which two exclusions do most of the work in practice?
recall.a: Normal course of business and another statutory obligation.

recall.q: What is the vanishing-company test?
recall.a: If the company disappeared tomorrow, would the activity still be worth doing for the people it serves?

recall.q: What turns most boundary disputes?
recall.a: How wide the beneficiary group really is.

sections.title: The Two Per Cent: how the obligation is computed
sections.big_idea: Take **three years of Section 198 profit**, average them, multiply by 2%. Then watch surplus, assets and overheads.
in_plain_words: The board must ensure the company spends at least 2% of the average net profit of the three immediately preceding financial years. The amount is fixed before the year starts. A company with fewer than three years averages the years it has. A loss-making year does not remove the obligation, and a company in scope with nil average profit owes a nil amount and still owes the governance.

Surplus from CSR activities never returns to the company. Excess spending can be set off against later years only with a board resolution. Assets built with CSR money must be held by a Section 8 company, trust or society with a track record, by beneficiaries, or by a public authority. Administrative overheads are capped at 5% of CSR expenditure. **The money is spent when it leaves, and it does not come back.**

diagram.note: set before the year begins: a company knows in April what it owes by March

key_terms.meaning: The minimum: 2% of three-year average net profit.
Carrying excess spending against up to three succeeding years, with a board resolution.
Interest, asset income or sale proceeds from CSR; must be ploughed back or transferred.
CSR-built assets must be held outside the company.
The company's own CSR running costs, capped at 5%.
The top ten spenders give about 17% of all CSR.

worked_example.title: Compute an obligation and its overhead cap
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's hypothetical figures: net profit ₹40 crore, ₹70 crore and ₹10 crore for FY 2023-24 to 2025-26. The obligation is for FY 2026-27.
steps: Three-year total: 40 + 70 + 10 = 120 crore.
Average: 120 ÷ 3 = 40 crore.
Obligation: 40 × 0.02 = 0.8 crore.
In lakh (1 crore is 100 lakh): 0.8 × 100 = 80 lakh.
Overhead cap if the company spends exactly 80 lakh: 80 × 0.05 = 4 lakh.
worked_example.answer: ₹80 lakh to be spent in FY 2026-27, with the company's own administrative overheads capped at ₹4 lakh.

mistakes: Computing the 2% on the latest year's profit instead of the three-year average.
Applying the 5% cap to an implementing partner's delivery cost, which is project expenditure.
Assuming excess spending creates a set-off automatically when a board resolution is required.
Letting the company keep the school building it built with CSR money.

recall.q: What is the prescribed CSR expenditure?
recall.a: At least 2% of the average net profit of the three immediately preceding financial years.

recall.q: What happens to CSR surplus?
recall.a: It is ploughed back into the same project, moved to the Unspent CSR Account, or transferred to a Schedule VII fund.

recall.q: Who may hold a CSR-built asset?
recall.a: A Section 8 company, trust or society with a track record, the beneficiaries as a collective, or a public authority.

recall.q: What does the 5% cap cover?
recall.a: The company's own cost of managing CSR; the implementing partner's delivery cost sits outside it.

recall.q: Which two heads take roughly seven rupees in ten?
recall.a: Health and education.

sections.title: The Board's Duty: Committee, action plan, certification
sections.big_idea: The committee sets policy and plan, the board approves and answers for it, and **the CFO certifies** the use of funds.
in_plain_words: A company in scope constitutes a CSR Committee of three or more directors including at least one independent director, or two or more where no independent director is required. Where the amount does not exceed ₹50 lakh the committee is not required, unless unspent money is held, and the board does its work. The committee formulates the policy, recommends the amount, monitors, and since 2021 formulates the annual action plan.

The board approves the policy, ensures activities and spending happen, and satisfies itself that funds were used as approved, with the CFO certifying. The company publishes the committee, policy and approved projects on its website. Penalties are civil since 2020. **The action plan is the first document an auditor reads**, and an unrecorded mid-year change is what gets written up.

key_terms.meaning: Board committee of three or more directors, one of them independent.
Annual list of projects, execution, funds, monitoring and assessment.
The finance head certifies funds were disbursed and used as approved.
Removes only the committee requirement for small obligations.
The penalty provision, civil since the 2020 amendment.
A statement of how the need was established, often skipped.

worked_example.title: Does the committee apply, and what is the penalty?
worked_example.setup: Two illustrative cases using the deck's rules. Company P has an obligation of ₹45 lakh. Company Q fails to transfer ₹2 crore of unspent money (penalty figures are the deck's; check the current text).
steps: P is under the ₹50 lakh limit: 50 − 45 = 5 lakh below it, so no committee, and the board does the work.
Q's company penalty: twice the amount, 2 × 2 = 4 crore, against a ceiling of ₹1 crore, whichever is less.
So Q is liable for ₹1 crore.
An officer in default: one-tenth of the amount, 2 ÷ 10 = 0.2 crore, against ₹2 lakh, whichever is less.
So each officer is liable for ₹2 lakh.
worked_example.answer: P needs no committee. Q owes ₹1 crore and each officer in default ₹2 lakh.

mistakes: Assuming the ₹50 lakh exemption removes the policy, plan, spend and report. It removes only the committee.
Treating the committee as the certifier, when certification is the CFO's duty.
Writing an action plan with projects and budgets but no statement of need.
Treating the penalty as a spending penalty when it attaches to failure to transfer unspent money.

recall.q: How many directors sit on the committee?
recall.a: Three or more, including one independent director; two or more if no independent director is required.

recall.q: Which three things must the website carry?
recall.a: Committee composition, the CSR policy and approved projects.

recall.q: Who certifies that funds were used as approved?
recall.a: The Chief Financial Officer or the person responsible for financial management.

recall.q: What changed in 2020?
recall.a: Non-compliance was decriminalised and imprisonment replaced by monetary penalty.

recall.q: Why does a reader want the action plan?
recall.a: It converts the policy into named projects with money, dates and a way of checking them.

sections.title: The Money That Did Not Move: Unspent CSR, and the 2021 machinery
sections.big_idea: Since 2021 the rule is **transfer or pay**. One question decides the route: is it an ongoing project?
in_plain_words: Before 2021, a company that did not spend explained itself in the board's report. Now unspent money must move. For an ongoing project it goes to the Unspent CSR Account, a separate bank account, within 30 days of year end, and must be spent within three financial years. For anything else it goes to a Schedule VII fund within six months.

An ongoing project is a defined term: multi-year, with a timeline of up to three years excluding the year of commencement. The three-year clock starts at transfer into the account, and any balance then goes to a Schedule VII fund within 30 days. Those funds are central: the PM National Relief Fund, PM CARES, Clean Ganga Fund and Swachh Bharat Kosh. **Labelling a project ongoing after the year closes does not make it so.**

children.label: Ongoing project
items: Balance to Schedule VII fund in 30 days

key_terms.meaning: A separate bank account for unspent money on ongoing projects.
A multi-year project with a timeline up to three years, excluding the first year.
A specified central fund, such as PM CARES or Clean Ganga Fund.
The limit after which unspent account money must move out.
The post-2021 regime: unspent money moves, or a penalty applies.

worked_example.title: Trace ₹30 lakh of unspent money
worked_example.setup: An illustrative company owes ₹80 lakh and spends ₹50 lakh. The rest is committed to an ongoing project; after three years it has spent ₹18 lakh of it.
steps: Unspent at year end: 80 − 50 = 30 lakh.
Within 30 days of year end it moves to the Unspent CSR Account.
After three financial years the amount left is 30 − 18 = 12 lakh.
That 12 lakh goes to a Schedule VII fund within 30 days.
If the project were not ongoing, the whole 30 lakh would go to a Schedule VII fund within six months.
worked_example.answer: 30 lakh unspent, of which 12 lakh ends in a Schedule VII fund after the third year.

mistakes: Using a pre-2021 guidance note, which treats unspent money as a disclosure item.
Dropping the commencement-year exclusion when counting the three years of an ongoing project.
Counting the three-year window from the project start when it runs from transfer into the account.
Sending unspent money to the NGO partner or a state fund, which the rules do not allow.

recall.q: What are the two deadlines for unspent money?
recall.a: 30 days for an ongoing project's transfer, and six months for a non-ongoing project's transfer to a fund.

recall.q: What is an ongoing project?
recall.a: A multi-year project with a timeline not exceeding three years excluding the commencement year.

recall.q: When does the three-year window start?
recall.a: From the transfer into the Unspent CSR Account.

recall.q: Name two funds that receive unspent money.
recall.a: Any two of: PM National Relief Fund, PM CARES, Clean Ganga Fund, Swachh Bharat Kosh.

recall.q: What did the 2020 amendment do to penalties?
recall.a: It converted the regime from criminal to civil.

sections.title: Who May Spend It: Implementation routes and CSR-1
sections.big_idea: Four routes deliver CSR. **No CSR-1, no corporate money** for an external organisation, and a three-year record is required.
in_plain_words: A company may deliver CSR itself, through its own foundation, through a government entity, or through an external Section 8 company, registered public trust or society with an established track record of at least three years. An entity the company sets up faces no track-record test, so the rule is strictest on partners the company does not control.

From 1 April 2021 an implementing entity must file Form CSR-1 electronically with the Registrar of Companies and obtain a registration number. The form needs 12A and 80G (or 10(23C)), entity type, governing body details, a digital signature and certification by a CA, CS or cost accountant. The board still answers for the money, and the CFO certifies. Companies may pool, if each can report separately. **Design utilisation certificates at proposal stage.**

key_terms.meaning: Form filed with the Registrar to obtain a CSR Registration Number.
A not-for-profit company, one eligible kind of implementer.
Income-tax registration and approval needed for CSR-1.
At least three years of similar work, required of external bodies.
A partner's record that funds were used as approved.
Companies funding one project together, each reporting separately.

worked_example.title: Pool ten small obligations
worked_example.setup: Ten illustrative companies each owe ₹30 lakh and pool the money for one district project, each able to report separately.
steps: Pooled amount: 10 × 30 = 300 lakh.
In crore (1 crore is 100 lakh): 300 ÷ 100 = 3 crore.
Each company's share of the pool: 30 ÷ 300 = 10%.
A 5% overhead cap across the pooled spend would be 300 × 0.05 = 15 lakh.
worked_example.answer: ₹3 crore for a district-scale project, with each company's share tracked at 10% and overheads capped at ₹15 lakh.

mistakes: Assuming a decade of work qualifies an NGO that never filed CSR-1.
Expecting the company's own foundation to face the same three-year test as an outside NGO.
Pooling funds in a way that hides which company's money did what.
Waiting until year end to assemble beneficiary records the CFO needs to certify.

recall.q: What are the four delivery routes?
recall.a: The company itself, its own foundation, a government entity, and an external organisation.

recall.q: When did CSR-1 registration become mandatory?
recall.a: From 1 April 2021.

recall.q: Who receives the CSR-1 filing?
recall.a: The Registrar of Companies, electronically.

recall.q: What track record must an external organisation have?
recall.a: At least three years in similar activities.

recall.q: What condition applies to pooled projects?
recall.a: Each company's CSR Committee must be able to report separately on the project.

sections.title: Does It Work? Impact assessment, and what it rarely asks
sections.big_idea: Assessment is mandatory only for **big spenders' big projects**, and the Rules set no method. Ask what would have happened anyway.
in_plain_words: An independent assessment is required where a company's average CSR obligation is ₹10 crore or more in the three preceding years and the project's outlay is ₹1 crore or more and completed at least a year earlier. Both limbs must be met. The cost can be booked to CSR under a cap that sits outside the 5% overhead limit.

The Rules require an independent agency but no methodology, qualification or accreditation. The report is placed before the board and annexed to the annual CSR report, so anyone can read it. Most report outputs, before-and-after values and satisfaction. **A before-and-after difference is not an impact estimate** without a comparison group and a statement of what would have happened anyway.

key_terms.meaning: Independent study of a project's effect, required above both limbs.
Average obligation of ₹10 crore or more, and project outlay of ₹1 crore or more.
What was delivered, such as people reached or units built.
What changed for people as a result.
A causal claim that needs a comparison.
What would have happened without the programme.

worked_example.title: Does a project need an assessment?
worked_example.setup: An illustrative company has CSR obligations of ₹10 crore, ₹12 crore and ₹14 crore in the three preceding years. It finished a ₹1.5 crore project 14 months ago.
steps: Total obligation: 10 + 12 + 14 = 36 crore.
Average obligation: 36 ÷ 3 = 12 crore, which is at least 10 crore.
Project outlay of 1.5 crore is at least 1 crore.
Time since completion: 14 − 12 = 2 months beyond the one-year minimum.
worked_example.answer: Both limbs are met, so an independent assessment is mandatory.

mistakes: Treating reach (40,000 people) as a result, when change needs a comparison.
Assuming the Rules guarantee quality. They require an independent agency but no method.
Accepting a report with no negative findings and no stated limitations as evaluation.
Assessing a project on completion, which measures delivery before effects appear.

recall.q: What are the two limbs for mandatory assessment?
recall.a: Average CSR obligation of ₹10 crore or more, and a project outlay of ₹1 crore or more completed at least a year before the study.

recall.q: Where is the assessment report published?
recall.a: Annexed to the annual report on CSR.

recall.q: Is assessment cost chargeable to CSR?
recall.a: Yes, up to a cap in Rule 8(3)(c), outside the 5% overhead limit.

recall.q: What distinguishes an output from an outcome?
recall.a: An output is what was delivered; an outcome is what changed.

recall.q: Name two features of a better assessment.
recall.a: Any two of: tests the theory of change, separates outputs from outcomes, states attribution, reports what failed, names limitations.

sections.title: From Spend To Disclosure: BRSR and the nine NGRBC principles
sections.big_idea: CSR asks what you spent. BRSR asks **how the whole business behaves**. Check assurance, boundary and baselines before you trust a number.
in_plain_words: The Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report is SEBI's mandatory ESG format for the top 1,000 listed entities from FY 2022-23, replacing the BRR. It rests on the nine principles of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct. Section A has general disclosures, Section B policies and governance, and Section C essential (mandatory) and leadership (voluntary) indicators.

BRSR Core is a subset of nine attributes that receive reasonable assurance, phased in by market-capitalisation rank. Assurance runs from none, to limited (negative comfort), to reasonable (a positive opinion). The common greenwashing moves are targets without baselines, intensity without absolutes, Scope 1 and 2 only, moved baselines and offsets counted as cuts. **The boundary question does the most work.**

diagram.root: How a BRSR is laid out
diagram.caption: three sections plus the assured subset

key_terms.meaning: SEBI's mandatory ESG disclosure format for the top 1,000 listed entities.
National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct: nine principles.
A mandatory BRSR question.
A voluntary BRSR question.
Nine assured attributes, phased in by market capitalisation.
A third party's check of a disclosed figure, at limited or reasonable level.

worked_example.title: Intensity falls while the total rises
worked_example.setup: An illustrative company reports emissions of 1,000 tonnes on revenue of ₹400 crore, then 1,080 tonnes on revenue of ₹480 crore.
steps: Old intensity: 1,000 ÷ 400 = 2.5 tonnes per crore.
New intensity: 1,080 ÷ 480 = 2.25 tonnes per crore.
Absolute increase: 1,080 − 1,000 = 80 tonnes.
Relative increase: 80 ÷ 1,000 = 8%.
worked_example.answer: Intensity fell from 2.5 to 2.25 while total emissions rose 8%. Ask for both figures.

mistakes: Treating CSR and BRSR as nested. A large unlisted company can be in Section 135 and file no BRSR.
Reading a headline figure without checking which entities the boundary includes.
Believing a number is checked when it carries no assurance or only limited assurance.
Accepting a Yes in Section B without a matching number in Section C.

recall.q: Who regulates BRSR, and who regulates CSR?
recall.a: SEBI regulates BRSR; the Ministry of Corporate Affairs regulates Section 135 CSR.

recall.q: Which principle covers public policy influence?
recall.a: Principle 7.

recall.q: Where is CSR reported within the BRSR?
recall.a: Under Principle 8, inclusive growth and equitable development.

recall.q: What is the difference between limited and reasonable assurance?
recall.a: Limited says nothing came to attention; reasonable gives a positive opinion that the figure is fairly stated.

recall.q: Which section of a BRSR should you read first?
recall.a: Section A, and keep it open.

sections.title: Where India Sits: GRI, TCFD, ISSB, CSRD, and the gap
sections.big_idea: Each framework was written for someone: **follow the question it declines to ask.** Materiality shows who it serves.
in_plain_words: ESG reporting grew from voluntary initiatives, so the field is crowded. GRI covers a company's impact on the world for all stakeholders. SASB covers financially material issues by industry for investors. TCFD covers climate risk. ISSB (IFRS S1 and S2) sets a global baseline, and CSRD with ESRS is mandatory EU reporting with double materiality.

BRSR descends from a government guideline, NGRBC, enforced by a securities regulator, so it asks about conduct and advocacy beside emissions. The SDGs have 17 goals, 169 targets and 234 indicators, yet corporate mapping stops at goals. Human rights due diligence and value chains are where reporting is thinnest. **An Indian supplier can meet CSRD through its customer.**

key_terms.meaning: What sustainability issues affect the company's value.
What effect the company has on people and environment.
Both questions together, the EU CSRD position.
UN Guiding Principles: protect, respect, remedy.
Suppliers, contractors and informal labour behind a company.
Emissions in the value chain, often most of the footprint.

worked_example.title: How thin is goal-level alignment?
worked_example.setup: A report claims to advance 8 of the SDGs. The deck gives 17 goals, 169 targets and 234 unique indicators.
steps: Share of goals claimed: 8 ÷ 17 = 47%.
Average targets per goal: 169 ÷ 17 = 9.9.
Average indicators per target: 234 ÷ 169 = 1.4.
The report names no target or indicator, so none of the 234 indicators is shown to have moved.
worked_example.answer: The claim covers 47% of goals, and each goal has about ten targets, so goal-level alignment says very little.

mistakes: Expecting every framework to ask the same question. Each was written for a different audience.
Treating SDG mapping as accountability when it costs nothing to assert at goal level.
Thinking CSR spending satisfies human rights due diligence, which is about harm the business causes.
Assuming CSRD is only an EU matter when it reaches Indian suppliers through customers.

recall.q: Which materiality does GRI use, and which do SASB and ISSB use?
recall.a: GRI uses impact materiality; SASB and ISSB use financial materiality.

recall.q: What does double materiality require?
recall.a: Both financial and impact questions, the EU CSRD position.

recall.q: How many SDG goals, targets and indicators are there?
recall.a: 17 goals, 169 targets and 234 unique indicators.

recall.q: What are the three pillars of the UNGPs?
recall.a: The state's duty to protect, the corporate responsibility to respect, and access to remedy.

recall.q: Where does BRSR descend from?
recall.a: A government guideline, NGRBC, enforced by a securities regulator.

sections.title: Reading It Critically: Ten questions, and how to stay current
sections.big_idea: A report is a claim by an interested party. **Read it as evidence**, with ten questions, and check the primary source for anything that changes.
in_plain_words: Few people draft Section 135 policies, and almost everyone has to read reports written by people with an interest in how they are read. The task is to separate what a document establishes from what it asserts. The ten questions cover boundary, amount, unspent money, named projects, implementer and CSR-1, counterfactual, assurance, baselines, Scope 3 and numbers against narrative.

Weak CSR reports are vague about what was done, and weak ESG reports are precise about the wrong thing. Thresholds, deadlines, forms and penalties have all been amended since 2014, so check mca.gov.in, csr.gov.in and sebi.gov.in directly. The csr.gov.in portal is open data on company spending, though it records disclosure and cannot audit delivery. **Settled law and contested judgement need separating.**

children.label: Money and projects
items: Which entities are in the boundary?
Is any amount unspent, and where?

diagram.caption: nine answerable from published documents, one needs judgement

key_terms.meaning: The entities a report includes.
A pattern worth a question; one is an oversight, four are a pattern.
The national CSR portal with company-level spending data.
Law checkable against a statute, such as scope and the 2% rule.
Open judgement, such as whether mandated CSR is good policy.

worked_example.title: Apply two of the ten questions
worked_example.setup: An illustrative report states a prescribed amount of ₹80 lakh and says ₹60 lakh was spent on named projects, with no mention of the rest.
steps: Unspent amount: 80 − 60 = 20 lakh.
Share of the obligation unspent: 20 ÷ 80 = 25%.
Question three asks where the 20 lakh went: the Unspent CSR Account or a Schedule VII fund.
Question two is also open until the arithmetic and the deadline are shown.
worked_example.answer: 25% of the obligation, ₹20 lakh, is unaccounted for until the report traces it.

mistakes: Reading a report as testimony when it is a claim by an interested party.
Quoting a threshold, penalty or deadline from an old guidance note as permanent.
Treating csr.gov.in as an audit of delivery when it records what companies filed.
Confusing firm legal requirements with open policy questions, in either direction.

recall.q: What is the core skill of the course?
recall.a: Separating what a document establishes from what it asserts.

recall.q: How many of the ten questions can be answered from published documents?
recall.a: Nine; only the last needs judgement.

recall.q: How do weak CSR reports and weak ESG reports differ?
recall.a: CSR reports are vague about what was done; ESG reports are precise about the wrong thing.

recall.q: Which four primary sources does the deck name for staying current?
recall.a: mca.gov.in, csr.gov.in, sebi.gov.in and the company's own website.

recall.q: Name one settled and one contested matter.
recall.a: Settled: how the 2% is computed. Contested: whether mandated CSR is good policy.

notes.2: Eleven sections move from why India has a legal CSR duty through scope, Schedule VII, the 2% calculation and board duties, then unspent money, delivery routes, impact assessment, BRSR and global frameworks. **The last section turns it all into ten questions** you can put to any report.
notes.4: Hold the key contrast: voluntary guidelines in 2009 and 2011 drew thin take-up, so the Companies Act 2013 made a minimum spend a statutory duty. In scope, CSR is compliance. **That changes who is accountable, what is documented and which deadlines apply**, and is why foreign CSR writing transfers poorly.
notes.5: The 2% is small for one firm (a company averaging ₹100 crore owes ₹2 crore) and large in total at ₹34,909 crore in FY2023-24. The easily forgotten part is the three-year window: **the obligation was fixed by profits already reported**, so CSR budgeting is a scheduling task.
notes.6: Use the three words as a sorting test. CSR is a duty under company law, ESG is a disclosure frame for investors, sustainability is a description. When a job advert or policy mixes them, it mixes **three obligations with three audiences**. Keeping them apart is the first practical skill.
notes.7: Learn the sequence as a ladder from encouragement to obligation: 2009 guidelines, 2011 NVGs, 2013 Act, 2014 commencement on 1 April, 2021 amendment rules. The 2021 line deserves a mark, since **it added unspent-money machinery, CSR-1 and impact assessment**. India followed Mauritius (2009).
notes.8: Read the two columns as different kinds of claim. The case for is about money reaching the sector and is mostly measurable. The case against is about who decides, which spending data cannot settle. **Work that challenges power fits Schedule VII poorly**, so note what the funding stream leaves out.
notes.9: These five abilities are the deck's learning outcomes, and each matches a real job: company secretary, finance team, programme manager, NGO, analyst. **Tick them off as you finish each section.** Slides that help with none of the five are context.
notes.11: Memorise three thresholds and the word 'any': net worth ₹500 crore, turnover ₹1,000 crore, net profit ₹5 crore, tested on the year just ended. **Reading the three as cumulative is the commonest error** and produces wrong advice that a company is exempt. A loss-making company with high net worth is in scope.
notes.12: Two windows, two questions. Scope reads one year, the year just ended. The amount reads the average of three preceding years. Draw a four-row table of years and **shade one row for scope and three for the amount**, since the two windows are routinely confused.
notes.13: Entry and exit are immediate: a company meeting none of the three thresholds in the preceding year is out for the next. Rule 3(2), the three-year lag, was omitted from 20 September 2022. One exception: **a company holding money in its Unspent CSR Account** must still keep a committee and comply with 135(2) to (6).
notes.14: Foreign branches and project offices are in scope on Indian figures, computed from the Section 381(1)(a) statements. A large multinational with a small Indian branch may owe nothing, while a mid-sized foreign firm with a big project office may be covered. **Size in India is what the section reads.**
notes.15: Net profit for CSR is the Section 198 figure, minus two exclusions: overseas-branch profit and dividends from Indian companies that are covered by and comply with Section 135. The second blocks double counting. **A dividend from an uncovered company stays in**, so look at each subsidiary in a mixed group.
notes.16: Work the four companies yourself before reading the right column. Test each against the three thresholds and stop at the first that is met. Beta is the lesson: a loss-making company in scope on turnover **owes nothing but must still constitute governance** and report. In scope and owing money are separate.
notes.17: Because any threshold binds, turnover or net worth usually decides, and profit matters less. A loss-making firm with turnover above ₹1,000 crore is covered. The profit threshold is the lowest bar and the one most often assumed to be the only one, so **check turnover and net worth first**.
notes.19: Treat Schedule VII as a gate: spending outside it is not CSR however worthy. The outline groups hunger and health, education and livelihood, gender and inequality, environment, heritage, veterans, sport, government funds, incubators and R&D, and rural and disaster work. **Read the Schedule itself before advising**, as the slide says.
notes.20: 'Liberally' means read each entry for its essence, and it does not mean anything goes. A water project can be rural development, sanitation or environment, and none of those readings is wrong. **Practise arguing a boundary case in writing**, naming the entry and its essence, because an auditor will look for that.
notes.21: Learn the six exclusions. The last two do most of the work: normal course of business and another statutory obligation. Between them they rule out much spending that is beneficial. **Ask of each project: is it outside India, staff-only, political, routine, marketing, or already required?**
notes.22: The hard cases follow one pattern: who is the beneficiary, and would this have been spent regardless? Almost everything on both lists is good. A skilling programme open to the wider community is probably CSR, and one that feeds only the company's hiring pipeline is probably not. **Apply the two questions** to each pair.
notes.23: Use the vanishing-company question as a quick screen: if the company disappeared tomorrow, would the activity still be worth doing for the people it serves? If the beneficiaries are the workforce or the supply chain, it is probably business expenditure. **Most disputes turn on how wide the beneficiary group is.**
notes.25: The formula has two key words. 'Average' smooths a bad or spectacular year, and 'preceding' fixes the amount before the year begins, so a company knows in April what it owes by March. A company with fewer than three years **averages the years it has**: in its second year, one year.
notes.26: Rework the table: add the three profits (40, 70, 10), divide by three for ₹40 crore, take 2% for ₹80 lakh. The obligation for FY 2026-27 is set by years already reported. The averaging cuts both ways: **a collapse to ₹10 crore does not remove the obligation**, and a spectacular year does not raise it at once.
notes.27: Zero profit does not erase the duties. A company in scope on turnover or net worth with nil average net profit owes a nil amount but still needs a committee or board process, a policy, an action plan and a report. **In scope sets the governance, and average profit sets the amount.**
notes.28: Surplus from a CSR project, including interest, income from a CSR asset or sale proceeds, never counts as company profit. It has three exits: back into the same project, to the Unspent CSR Account, or to a Schedule VII fund. **The money cannot return to the company**, which closes the route to a revenue line.
notes.29: Set-off lets a company that overspends carry the excess against later years, because CSR spending is lumpy and the obligation is annual. Conditions include board approval and a limit on how far forward it carries. **Read the current text of Rule 7 before advising**, as the slide warns.
notes.30: Ownership follows the asset. CSR-built assets must sit with a Section 8 company, registered trust or society with a track record, with beneficiaries as a self-help group or collective, or with a public authority. A school building that stays the company's property is **a corporate asset and no contribution**. Pre-2021 assets had 180 days to transfer.
notes.31: The 5% cap covers the company's own cost of running CSR: CSR staff salaries, office costs, programme audit. It excludes the implementing partner's delivery cost, which is project expenditure. **An NGO told its overheads are capped at 5% has been given the wrong rule.** Impact assessment sits outside the cap.
notes.32: Section 198 starts from the profit and loss account and then adds back and deducts specified items. The lists show what gets no credit (share premium, capital profits, revaluation surplus) and which deductions apply. Remember the two exclusions most used in practice: **overseas-branch profit and dividends from covered companies**.
notes.33: Set-off has three conditions: the excess must not include CSR surplus, the board must pass a resolution, and the credit carries for up to three succeeding years. The resolution is the operative step: **a company that overspends without resolving to carry forward has simply overspent.**
notes.34: Slide 30 gave the rule and this slide gives the three holders: a Section 8 company, trust or society with CSR-1, the beneficiaries as a self-help group or collective, or a public authority. The rule attaches to the asset. **Check that the holder can maintain it and bear its running costs.**
notes.35: Hold three figures: ₹34,909 crore total CSR in FY2023-24, the 2% rate, and the comparison with ₹95,692 crore for the rural employment guarantee in Budget 2026-27. CSR is about a third of that one scheme. **It is a real funding stream and cannot replace public spending.**
notes.36: Read the chart for its shape: health and education together take roughly seven rupees in ten, and every other Schedule VII head shares the remaining 29%. The slide explains this as thousands of corporate decisions that **cluster on what is legible and uncontroversial**. The split reflects company choices and says little about need.
notes.37: Ten firms give about ₹5,880 crore, roughly 17% of all CSR. Segment funders in your head: a top-ten spender can fund a programme outright, while a company with a ₹40 lakh obligation needs a partner who absorbs a small grant with light reporting. **Confusing the two conversations wastes everyone's time.**
notes.38: Convert the table to rupees: health and sanitation 38.4%, education and skilling 32.4%, environment 10.9%, rural development 6.9%, all others 11.4%. If your cause sits outside the top two, **you compete for a smaller pool than Schedule VII suggests**. Disability, legal aid and care work sit in the 'other' share.
notes.39: The league table names the ten largest spenders, HDFC Bank at ₹945 crore down to ICICI Bank at ₹368 crore. Together they give about ₹5,880 crore. Before approaching a company, **check which kind of funder it is**: a few write cheques big enough to fund a programme.
notes.41: Count directors: three or more with at least one independent, or two or more where no independent director is required. The ₹50 lakh exemption removes only the committee. The board still adopts the policy, the plan, the spend and the report. **The exemption lapses for a company holding unspent money.**
notes.42: Learn the committee's three functions (policy, amount, monitoring) plus the action plan added in 2021. The right column lists what it does not do. The key point: **the CFO certifies use of funds, so the person who signs did not set the policy**.
notes.43: The five board duties run from approving the policy to explaining any shortfall. Read duty four closely: the board must satisfy itself funds were utilised for the approved purposes and manner, which goes beyond disbursement. **CFO certification is why partners are asked for utilisation certificates and beneficiary records.**
notes.44: The action plan turns an aspirational policy into projects, execution method, funding schedules, monitoring and assessment details. It is the first document an auditor reads. The board may alter it during the year with reasons recorded. **The undocumented change is what gets written up**, and the change itself is allowed.
notes.45: Know the three public items: the annual CSR report in the board's report, and on the website the committee composition, the CSR policy and approved projects. Impact assessments are annexed where they apply. Because it is public, **you can read the primary document yourself** and compare plan with reported spend.
notes.46: This slide extends slide 44: projects are mapped to Schedule VII heads and the plan states direct or agency execution. The most skipped item is need assessment. A plan with projects and budgets but no statement of how need was established is **complete on its face and hollow underneath**.
notes.47: The 2020 Act replaced prison with money: the company pays twice the amount it should have transferred or ₹1 crore, whichever is less, and each officer in default one-tenth or ₹2 lakh, whichever is less. The penalty attaches to failing to transfer, so **spending nothing but transferring correctly is a different position**. Check current figures.
notes.48: The slide sets out the policy argument in two lists. For: predictable money, a board conversation, a public record, private profit directed to public purposes. Against: a tax without parliamentary control, no democratic mandate, easy-to-report spending, an arbitrary 2%. **Be able to argue either side.**
notes.50: Before 2021 an underspending company explained itself in the board's report. After 2021 it must move the money, with deadlines of 30 days and six months and a three-year backstop. **Check the date of any guidance note**: anything earlier than 2021 treats unspent money wrongly.
notes.51: The fork is one question: is it an ongoing project? If yes, move the unspent amount to the Unspent CSR Account within 30 days and spend it within three financial years. If no, move it to a Schedule VII fund within six months. **Deciding after year-end that a project was ongoing changes nothing.**
notes.52: 'Ongoing project' is a defined term: multi-year, timeline up to three years excluding the commencement year. A project originally approved as single-year can become ongoing if the board extends it beyond a year with justification recorded. **Keep the commencement-year exclusion in your count**, the commonest arithmetic slip here.
notes.53: The three-year clock starts when money enters the Unspent CSR Account, and the project's start date plays no part. At the end of three financial years any balance goes to a Schedule VII fund within 30 days. So **a slipping project can run out of window while still running**. Draw the four boxes.
notes.54: Memorise the destination: only central funds, such as the PM National Relief Fund, PM CARES, Clean Ganga Fund and Swachh Bharat Kosh. No state fund, local body or NGO is allowed. The slide offers two readings: it stops underspending evaporating, or it **converts a corporate management failure into central revenue**.
notes.55: The 2020 Act made the regime civil. Read this as a redesign: a monetary penalty on the transfer duty targets the behaviour the state wants, which is that unspent money must leave the company. The slide says criminal liability for a budgeting shortfall chilled boards. **Read the current Section 135(7)** before quoting a figure.
notes.56: Use the table as a decision tree: an ongoing project goes to a separate bank account within 30 days, then to a Schedule VII fund within three financial years; a non-ongoing project goes direct to a Schedule VII fund within six months. **The first account must be a separate bank account**, with the money physically moved.
notes.58: Four routes: the company itself, its own foundation, a government entity, or an external organisation with a three-year record. The choice trades control for capacity. Note the asymmetry: **the company's own foundation faces no track-record test**, while an independent NGO does. The rule is strictest on partners the company does not control.
notes.59: CSR-1 is a one-time electronic filing with the Registrar of Companies from 1 April 2021, issuing a CSR Registration Number that every funder quotes. For an NGO it is the practical gate. **No CSR-1 means no corporate money**, however good the organisation or long its work.
notes.60: Prepare the CSR-1 file: 12A and 80G (or 10(23C)), entity type, governing body details, PAN and certificate, digital signature, and certification by a CA, CS or cost accountant. Filing carries no fee, and the certifying professional attests to eligibility, including the three-year record. **Check the current form** on the MCA portal first.
notes.61: Three years of track record prevents shell intermediaries, untested entities with large first grants and agencies with no record to check. It also costs: new organisations and community-rooted groups wait three years. **A company's own foundation faces a lower bar** than an independent NGO, and the slide calls both effects real.
notes.62: Responsibility stays with the company: the board satisfies itself, and the CFO or person responsible for finance certifies. For an NGO, translate that into utilisation certificates, beneficiary records and audit trails. **Design these at proposal stage**, since the CFO cannot certify what was never recorded.
notes.63: Pooling suits small obligations: most covered companies owe a few lakh to a few crore, enough for a fragment of a programme. Ten pooled obligations can fund a district-level intervention. The condition is separate reporting, so **the implementing agency must keep each company's money attributable**.
notes.64: CSR-1 requires an eligible entity (Section 8 company, registered public trust or society), 12A and 80G or 10(23C) with 80G, a three-year record and professional certification. Read the four together: **formally registered, tax-compliant, audited and three years old**. A company cannot waive the three-year condition.
notes.66: Two limbs, both required: average CSR obligation of ₹10 crore or more over three preceding years, and a project outlay of ₹1 crore or more completed at least a year earlier. The one-year gap lets effects appear. **Mandatory assessment reaches only big spenders' big projects**; everything else is voluntary or absent.
notes.67: Impact assessment cost can be booked to CSR for that year, subject to a cap in Rule 8(3)(c). That matters because evaluation is usually the first line cut. The cap sits outside the 5% overhead limit, so a company need not choose between **running its CSR function and evaluating it**. Check the current figure.
notes.68: The Rules require an independent agency and set no method, qualification or accreditation. The weakness is no floor and a company that selects and pays the evaluator. The opportunity is that nothing stops rigour. **Quality depends on whether the commissioning company wanted to find something out.**
notes.69: Use the five items as a checklist for reading any assessment: theory of change tested, outputs distinguished from outcomes, attribution explicit, negative findings reported, limitations named. None needs a randomised trial. **A report with no negative findings and no stated limitations reads as persuasion.**
notes.70: Separate reach (an output), change (an outcome) and attribution (a claim about causation needing a comparison). A report that says 40,000 people were reached has not shown change. The honest sentence costs nothing: **say plainly that the study cannot separate the programme's effect** from everything else happening.
notes.71: The assessment report goes before the board and is annexed to the annual CSR report, so anyone can read it. Quality ranges from competent evaluation to a brochure with a cover page, and both satisfy the rule. **Hundreds are published every year** and few are read systematically, which makes them a research resource.
notes.72: Most published assessments report outputs, before-and-after values and satisfaction. What would answer the question is a comparison group, an explicit statement of what would have happened anyway, and attention to attrition. **A before-and-after difference is an impact estimate only when alternative explanations are ruled out.**
notes.74: Contrast the regimes row by row: CSR is a spending obligation on the CSR budget, aimed at MCA, the board and the public, and applies over the Section 135 thresholds; BRSR is a disclosure obligation on the whole business for SEBI and investors. **They overlap but do not nest**, and the 2% is where the harm is least likely to sit.
notes.75: BRSR is SEBI's mandatory format for the top 1,000 listed entities, from FY 2022-23, replacing the BRR. The change of name marks wider scope: quantitative environmental and social data in a comparable structure. **This is the fastest-moving part of the subject**, so confirm applicability on sebi.gov.in.
notes.76: Learn the nine principles as a list, because Sections B and C follow them. The wording runs from integrity and safe products through employees, stakeholders, human rights, environment, policy advocacy and inclusive growth to consumers. **Recite them in order**, as the numbering recurs in every BRSR.
notes.77: A is general disclosures, B is policies and governance against each principle, C is performance with essential (mandatory) and leadership (voluntary) indicators. A company answering only essential indicators is complying and not leading. **Count which leadership indicators were answered and which left blank** to see the difference.
notes.78: Assurance has levels. None means the company asserts the number. Limited means nothing came to the assurer's attention (negative comfort). Reasonable means a positive opinion that the figure is fairly stated. **Ask of any ESG number: assured, and at what level?** BRSR Core phases in assurance by market-capitalisation rank.
notes.79: Use the tells as a checklist: targets with no baseline, intensity metrics only, Scope 3 omitted, 'committed to' without a date. The checks reverse them. **The boundary question does the most work**: a headline figure can be true and useless if subsidiaries are excluded. The reader got a different company.
notes.80: The nine principles each carry mandatory essential and voluntary leadership indicators. Principle 7 surprises people because it asks about trade bodies joined and positions advocated. Principle 8 is where CSR itself is reported. **The other eight describe how the business operates**, so BRSR is wider than its CSR section.
notes.81: BRSR Core is nine attributes chosen to be quantitative and comparable, which get reasonable assurance: greenhouse gas, water, energy, waste, employee wellbeing, gender diversity, inclusive development, fairness to customers and suppliers, openness of business. Assurance is expensive, so it covers **where a wrong number would most mislead an investor**.
notes.82: Greenwashing usually uses a true number chosen carefully. Check intensity against absolute emissions, Scope 3 against Scope 1 and 2, a moved baseline year, targets without interim milestones, and offsets counted as reductions. Each has a defensible rationale, so **look for whether every choice runs the same way** before accusing.
notes.83: With limited time, read Section A first and keep it open: turnover, employees and plants set the scale. Then compare Section B against Section C. **A policy answered yes in B with no number in C exists on paper.** BRSR Core marks the audited figures.
notes.85: Read the audience column first: GRI is for people affected by a company, SASB and ISSB for investors, TCFD for climate risk, CSRD for EU regulators and investors. Purpose chooses the topics and materiality test, so a company can look responsible under one frame and ordinary under another. **Confirm current status**, as consolidation continues.
notes.86: Financial materiality asks what affects the company's value (SASB, ISSB). Impact materiality asks what the company does to people and environment (GRI). Water use can be financially immaterial and the most material fact for a village. **Follow the question a standard declines to ask** to see who it was written for.
notes.87: BRSR descends from a government guideline (NGRBC) enforced by a securities regulator, so it asks about conduct and policy advocacy beside emissions. Learn it in that order: NGRBC first, since its principles carry across to GRI more readily than the reverse. **BRSR Core pushes it towards investor-grade comparability.**
notes.88: The SDGs have 17 goals, 169 targets and 234 unique indicators, yet corporate mapping stops at the goal. Goal-level alignment costs nothing to assert. When a report claims eight SDGs, **ask which indicator, at which target, moved by how much**. Silence is informative.
notes.89: The UNGPs rest on three pillars: the state's duty to protect, the company's responsibility to respect, and access to remedy for both. Human rights due diligence is about harm the business causes. **CSR spending satisfies none of the three**, because it concerns benefit conferred. NGRBC Principle 5 carries this.
notes.90: Own operations rarely hold the worst impacts. They sit in suppliers, contractors and informal labour: Scope 3, supplier labour conditions and contract-worker safety. A report that stops at the company gate leaves out most of the workforce. **CSRD makes the value chain explicit, and BRSR's treatment is the part most often called thin.**
notes.91: Compare BRSR with CSRD/ESRS row by row: driver (SEBI listing rule against EU law), materiality (single against double), assurance (reasonable on Core against limited), value chain (limited against explicit). **The obligation can arrive through your customer** if an Indian supplier serves a firm in CSRD scope.
notes.93: This is the core skill: read a report as a claim by an interested party in a format it helped design, and treat it as evidence. That assumes no bad faith. The task is to separate what the document establishes from what it asserts. **The law is the equipment; reading is the job.**
notes.94: Use the ten questions as a checklist: boundary, prescribed amount, unspent money, named projects, implementer and CSR-1, counterfactual, assurance, baselines and dates, Scope 3, and numbers against narrative. **Nine can be answered from published documents**, and the tenth needs judgement, where findings usually appear.
notes.95: Weak CSR reports fail by being vague about what was done. Weak ESG reports fail by being precise about the wrong thing. A beneficiary count with no definition and an intensity figure with no absolute are the same move. **One tell is an oversight; four together are a pattern.**
notes.96: Thresholds, deadlines, forms, penalty amounts and BRSR applicability have all changed since 2014. Bookmark the four primary sources: mca.gov.in, csr.gov.in, sebi.gov.in and the company's own website. **A five-minute check of the primary source** outlasts any secondary summary, including this deck.
notes.97: csr.gov.in publishes company-level spending by year, sector and state. The questions to try: which sectors get the most money, whether spending follows need or head offices, and which companies report large obligations and small spends. **The portal records disclosure and cannot audit delivery.**
notes.98: Sort the field into settled and contested. Settled: scope, the 2% computation, Schedule VII contents, unspent money rules, BRSR contents. Contested: whether mandated CSR is good policy, Schedule VII boundaries, impact assessment practice, ESG's effect, the 2% figure. **Treat firm law as firm and open questions as open.**
notes.99: Pick your next step by purpose. To commission or read assessments, take the MEL flagship and the two studios. To raise CSR funds, take the 101 course on how development funding is structured. Climate Essentials 101 supplies the science behind the E in ESG. **The interactive CSR map** behind Section 04's figures is worth an hour.
